newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kohl says Germans attached to mark but want euro.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Germans attached to mark but want euro.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said in a French television interview that Germans felt a strong attachment to their currency but that most believed it was more important to unite Europe through a single currency.

"...The great majority of Germans have a certain nostalgia when they talk about abandoning the deutschemark, but they have understood that peace, freedom and togetherness in Europe are more important than anything else," he told TF1 television.
A transcript of the interview was sent to Reuters before airtime.

"The deutschemark was there before we even had the Federal Republic, before we had a flag or a national anthem...When the deutschemark began, most of the gurus -- who were just as dumb then as they are today -- said it would never work. Then the deutschemark became an important currency. Now the Germans are saying, especially to me: 'And now we are supposed to give up the good old deutschemark?'

"And I say along with many other people in Germany, including incidentally the vast majority of German industry which wants the euro -- and that's important: 'I tell you...to build the European house we need a common currency, and that is the euro'," Kohl said.
He predicted political candidates in Germany who campaigned against monetary union in the next election would lose.

"...Anyone who tries to run the next election campaign against the euro, and thus against European unification -- and there are such voices among the Social Democrats -- will lose this election spectacularly," he said.

Kohl skirted some of the contentious issues relating to monetary union, such as how many EU members should be included in the first wave and whether a political counterweight should be established alongside a new European central bank.
He said Germany's experience and that of other countries showed it was preferable for central banks to be independent.

Asked to comment on the debate over whether some sort of "European economic government" was needed along with the European Central Bank, Kohl said, "I find this debate totally unnecessary. We have had an independent Bundesbank for many years, and it is really independent. It hasn't done the Germans, or the deutschemark, any harm and we will now have a European central bank.

"But this central bank isn't on the moon, it is in the middle of Europe and those who sit on it know the realities of Europe such as the job market, economic development and inflation rates. Why should that not work?
"I don't have this mistrust, not at all," he said.
He said he wanted to see as many European Union countries as possible fulfilling the criteria for European monetary union.
"And naturally I would like as many founder members (of the EU) as possible to meet the criteria. But it's not up to me, especially as a German, to give others advice," he said.

Pressed about whether European monetary union should group a large number of countries from the outset or a small group possibly excluding Italy, he said, "I think this whole debate is totally wrong, and I won't take part in it. Let each do his homework and then we'll talk about it next spring..."
